1.founded_by: the strait-pilots of the western shore
1.history: Caol leathan grew on the wide strait that gives it its name, where the western pilots of the Holy Age took a toll from every boat bound for the capital's waters. Its walls and citadel were raised in the Age of Sundering to hold the strait, and were manned again when the strangers' ships began to use it after the Crossing. It is the northern anchor of the Direwolf country, and its priests look south to the temple at Inis thais for their rite.
1.known_for: strait tolls and the western pilots' guild

2.history: An island town on the Abhainn fhionn, settled in the long quiet centuries by boatmen from Seann Vell upriver, Inis mhòr was walled once the capital's eastern approaches became worth defending. A' chiad rèisimeid, raised in the campaign of An Cogadh Fada, is stationed here and bears the town's name. Its barracks now outsize the old fishing quarter, and it lies within sight of the temple town of Cuan uaine, a little downriver; what it ships goes down the river to Cathair dhomhain.

3.founded_by: farming kindreds of the south-eastern downs
3.history: Baile ghorm is the market of its shire, a large open town without walls where the south-eastern farms bring their grain and wool. Its people keep the oldest folk rite, and household shrines to the ancestors outnumber any public house of worship. Achadh fhionn is its nearest field-village, and the ruin of Làrach an Dùin stands in its hinterland, left alone by custom.

4.founded_by: Ròdaich herders of the black-soil fields
4.history: Named for the dark earth of its fields, Baile dhubh was an ordinary Ròdaich farm town until the Severance drew the northern border around it. It kept its people when the province of Cnoc ghorm passed to the Tuathaich, and has lived since as a place of exchange and quiet mutual suspicion. Its folk hold the Yellow Scorpion faith, as their northern neighbours do, which is thought to be why they were left in peace.
4.known_for: Ròdaich enclave on the Tuathaich border

5.founded_by: Ròdaich woodsmen of the Holy Age
5.history: An oak-grove village of the Holy Age, Doire mhin was emptied of its Ròdaich families in the years of the Severance and filled by Tuathaich households moved north. It is a large village for its kind, living on the smooth-barked oaks that name it. Its timber goes down to the yards of Caol mhòr, and its people keep the Yellow Scorpion faith.
5.known_for: oak timber for the Caol mhòr yards

6.founded_by: river traders of the northern country
6.history: Cuan bheag, the small harbour, is a river port on the upper Abhainn ìseal. It was a fishing water until the Age of Strangers, when human traders wanted a sheltered mooring on this side of the island, with the river open to the sea at Ros gheal, and made it busy. The restored kingdom built its citadel to watch the northern approaches, and the town has since become one of the larger river ports of the province. Its people keep the capital's faith of the Dark Unicorn.
6.known_for: sheltered river mooring and the northern watch

7.founded_by: well-keepers of the north-eastern shore road
7.history: Tobar bhàn is a well village on the north-eastern shore road, named for a spring whose water runs white with chalk. The beacon of Taigh-solais Àth dhearg stands on the coast beyond it, and through the later Age of Strangers the village kept the lamp-keepers in bread and peat. Its people hold to the ancestors and the weather, and still leave a cup at the well before a sea-journey.
7.known_for: white well and the lighthouse keepers

8.history: Dùn thais, the damp fort, is a hill stronghold above the western coast, held by custodians of the vein's western road since the Holy Age. Its walls were rebuilt in the Age of Strangers, when the western harbours began shipping ore, and its citadel has never stood empty since. In An Cogadh Fada its garrison marched to the field of Àth leathan, a short road to the north-east.
8.known_for: hill citadel of the western coast

9.founded_by: Ròdaich harbour-folk; resettled by the Tuathaich
9.history: Inis mhin was a Ròdaich island harbour of the long quiet centuries, and its citadel was raised in the Age of Strangers by human administrators guarding the northern landing. After the Severance it passed wholly to the Tuathaich, and it is now one of their chief ports. It is among the coastal towns where the First Canoe fragment is still told, and the Tuathaich folk tradition holds here rather than the Yellow Scorpion faith of its neighbours.
9.known_for: Tuathaich port where the First Canoe is told

10.founded_by: river fishers of the Abhainn uaine
10.history: Cuan dhearg is one of the ring of small river towns on the Abhainn uaine above Cathair mhòr, named for the red cliffs over its landing. It lives on the river fish and the short ferry runs between the river towns, and sends what it has for the sea down to Ceann leathan at the river mouth. It has never been walled. It is not the southern Cuan dhearg that Tonn Mhòr destroyed; the chroniclers have confused the two more than once.

11.founded_by: hill shepherds of the northern coast
11.history: Cnoc ghlas is a hill town of the northern coast, a sheepwalk settlement of the Holy Age that later opened quarries in the grey slate of its hill. Its slate roofs much of the province of Tobar fhiadhaich. Its people follow Feallsanachd an Fhèidh, and the town sent more than its share of students to the school's revival.

12.history: Àth fhiadhaich stands at the ford where the eastern road meets the sea at a wild river mouth, and it has been a harbour since the Holy Age. It grew great on the traffic of the vein country in the Age of Strangers, and the famous tavern An Sligeanach Fad' às stands at Ceann bhàn, a short way down the road. The town keeps the oldest folk rite, and its fishing fleet still blesses its nets at the ford.
12.known_for: river-mouth harbour of the eastern road

13.founded_by: Ròdaich herders on an older field
13.history: Achadh àrsaidh, the ancient field, was named by Ròdaich herders who found its field-walls already standing and old when they came. No record says who laid them. Tiormachd Achadh shean, the Long Drought, struck it in the Age of Strangers and parched its hay-meadows for three dry seasons running. It has stayed a small village of cattle and hay on the eastern uplands, keeping the ancestor rite and its walls in repair.

14.history: The landing stones at Seann Chwen are of the Seann-Dhaoine, and the name was given by the Ròdaich who resettled the site in the Holy Age. It is a small harbour on the south shore, but its citadel guards the capital's southern sea road, and it has been garrisoned more often than its size would suggest. Its people keep the capital's faith of the Dark Unicorn, and its green is one of the two grounds where the travelling circus, An Siorcas Siubhail Do-thuigsinn, pitches.
14.known_for: citadel on the capital's southern sea road

15.founded_by: Ròdaich fishers of the red strait
15.history: Caol ruadh takes its name from the red rock of the strait it watches on the southern coast. It was a quiet fishing town for most of its history, and was among the first to take up the orthodox Obsidian Rite when Creideamh nan Ròdach was formalized. Since An Cogadh Fada its harbour has victualled the garrisons and fleet stationed at Seann Skell close by.
15.known_for: red strait and the orthodox Rite

16.history: Seann Skell is a Seann-Dhaoine harbour on the far north-west coast, named by the Ròdaich who resettled it; it passed to the Tuathaich after the Severance. Its citadel looks out over the waters where pirate ships are still reported and where old sailors place the Sea-Watcher. It is not the Seann Skell whose name the regiments carry, which lies far to the south-east.

17.history: Inis mhòr of the north-east is the great river port of its province, on the Abhainn ghorm, a fishing town of the Holy Age that became a city under the Age of Strangers' trade; its barges run down the river to Ros chiar at the mouth. Its people follow Feallsanachd an Fhèidh, and the town's debating halls were among the first to reopen at the school's revival. It shares the river and coastal trade with Ceann bheag and the walled town of Baile Mòr dhìreach inland.
17.known_for: north-eastern river fleet and debating halls

18.history: Seann Dunn keeps a Seann-Dhaoine name, and its citadel stands on footings no Ròdaich mason laid. It stands on the Abhainn chaol a little above the river mouth, and is the river landing and lodging-place for those who visit Làrach an Teampaill in the hills to the north, whose ships put in at Seann Mhorn down the coast; its own temple serves the ancestor rite. An Taigh-seinnse Òir, one of the great taverns of the old mining circuit, stands in the town itself.
18.known_for: An Taigh-seinnse Òir and the temple road

19.founded_by: the custodian-kings of the Holy Age
19.history: Cathair dhearg, the red city, began as the stone-walled seat of the Holy Age custodians where the mining roads came down to the sea on the Abhainn dhomhain; Drochaid Cathair dhearg, heir of the first bridges, still carries the road across the river. It kept its walls, citadel and temple through the Sundering and the Age of Strangers, and after the Severance Rìoghachd Ròdais was declared here and Niall was crowned in it, first of the restored line. The royal precinct is small for a capital, ringed by the great harbours of Ros dhomhain, Cathair dhomhain and Baile ghlas, and its temple is the first house of Uallach, the Dark Unicorn.
19.known_for: royal seat and temple of the Dark Unicorn

20.founded_by: hill kindreds of the north-central country
20.history: Cnoc bheag is the small hill only in name: it is the largest town of the north-central country, a river port on the Abhainn ìseal whose barges run down to Ros gheal on the coast, and the heart of the Hawk's congregations. The standing stone Carragh Cnoc bheag, carved 'there was fire in the stone', stands a short walk to the south, and the town's older families say their fathers' fathers found it there. A' Phlàigh Uaine, the Green Death, struck the town in the Age of Strangers. Since the Severance it has faced the Tuathaich border, and An siathamh rèisimeid, raised in An Cogadh Fada, is stationed here under the town's name.
20.known_for: the carved stone and the Sixth Regiment

21.history: Cnoc bhàn grew as an overflow of the harbour at Caol ìseal, a white hill with a landing at its foot. Its boats work the kelp beds and the herring of the northern shore. It keeps the ancestor rite and has never needed walls.

22.history: Ceann leathan, the broad headland, is a walled temple city on the gulf, older than most of the harbours around it. Its temple of the Dark Unicorn is the chief shrine of the gulf towns. Since the early years of the restored kingdom it has held Còmhrag Ceann leathan, the brutal annual melee, which draws fighters and crowds from every province.
22.known_for: Còmhrag Ceann leathan, the annual melee

23.founded_by: Ròdaich custodians of the interior roads
23.history: Cathair mhòr, the great city, was raised by the Holy Age custodians beside Làrach an Dùin-fhaire, a Seann-Dhaoine outpost already in ruins when the first Ròdaich walls went up beside it. It commands the roads between the gulf and the vein country, and it was a counting-house of the tithe in the Age of Strangers and a mustering place in the war that ended it. An treas rèisimeid, raised in An Cogadh Fada, is stationed here and bears its name.
23.known_for: the great city beside the old outpost

24.founded_by: Ròdaich fishers of the white headland
24.history: Ros gheal, Ros leathan and Seann Skell share one bay on the north-central coast, and have quarrelled over its moorings for as long as the rolls run. Ros gheal is the largest of the three and the seat of its province. Its people keep the Hawk's rite of Mòd, and its white headland is the first land the northern fishing boats see coming home.
24.known_for: white headland and the disputed bay

25.history: Inis ìseal is a low island in the Abhainn ìseal above Cnoc bheag, fortified in the long quiet centuries to guard that town's river and walled again in the Age of Strangers. Since the Severance it has been a frontier fortress facing the Tuathaich border, supplied by boats that come up the river from Ros gheal. The Green Death, A' Phlàigh Uaine, struck its garrison in the Age of Strangers, and it is a city by rank and a barracks in practice.

26.founded_by: Ròdaich shipwrights of the river mouth
26.history: Cathair dhomhain, the deep city, stands beside the capital on the deep-water side of the river mouth, and takes the ships whose draught the royal quays cannot. It was walled and given a citadel in the Holy Age, and its temple of the Dark Unicorn is second only to the capital's. Its harbour carried much of the ore trade in the Age of Strangers and most of the dubhan trade since.

27.founded_by: merchant families of the capital shore
27.history: Ros dhomhain is the most populous place of the capital country, a merchant port that outgrew every wall it was ever given until no one built another. The first human traders lodged here after the Crossing, and its counting-houses have served every master of the island's trade since. It sits between the capital and the old harbour of Seann Vell, and the three have run together into one shore.
27.known_for: the capital country's great merchant port

28.founded_by: Ròdaich shepherds; resettled by the Tuathaich
28.history: Cnoc àrsaidh is a hill village of the Holy Age crowned by a cairn older than its name. Its Ròdaich families went south at the Severance and Tuathaich households took their holdings. It is a small place of hill pasture, looking down on the harbour of Caol mhòr.
28.known_for: hill pasture and the old cairn

29.history: Seann Vell on the capital shore stands on Seann-Dhaoine quay stones, still visible at low water beneath the later harbour. The Ròdaich resettled it in the Holy Age and walled it in the long quiet centuries. It has since been drawn into the sprawl of Ros dhomhain, but keeps its own walls and its own harbour-master.
29.known_for: old quay stones of the capital shore

30.history: Ceann mhin is a citadel harbour on the southern gulf shore, long the chief shipyard of the east. When Tonn Mhòr struck in the first years of the restored kingdom, its yards were spared and it took in the survivors of Achadh mhin. It has since grown into one of the great cities of the south.

31.history: Cnoc mhòr is the market hill below Cathair mhòr, where the interior drove roads meet. It was walled in the Age of Strangers, when the city's markets spilled out to it. It is a prosperous town that keeps the capital's faith and sells the gulf its beef.

32.history: The northern of the two Àth shean holds the old ford where the road east from the capital crosses its river. It was walled in the Holy Age to guard that crossing and has grown into a large town. An Taigh-seinnse Mòr stands a short way up the road toward Seann Vell.
32.known_for: old ford of the eastern road

33.history: Ros ruadh is a small harbour on the gulf, founded by quarrymen who shipped its red stone to the gulf cities. Much of Ceann leathan and Ros bhàn is built of it. It keeps a ferry to the harbours across the water.
33.known_for: red stone for the gulf cities

34.history: Seann Tarr is a Seann-Dhaoine site on the north-eastern coast, resettled by the Ròdaich in the Holy Age, and its temple is one of the oldest houses of the ancestor rite still in use. A citadel was raised over the harbour in the Age of Sundering. It is small for a city, but the shrine draws the whole north-east at the great feasts.

35.founded_by: woodcutters of the wild oak wood
35.history: Doire fhiadhaich was a wild oak wood on the capital shore, and tradition holds that timber for the Sundering fleet was felled here. The wood is long gone and the village is now a fishing quarter between Ros dhomhain and the capital's harbours. It has kept its village rank and its own fishing rights.
35.known_for: oaks said to have built the Sundering fleet

36.history: The larger Seann Chwen is the chief harbour of the gulf and the seat of the province that bears its name, built on a Seann-Dhaoine site the Ròdaich resettled in the Holy Age. It takes the fish of the gulf and the goods of Cathair mhòr. It has no walls; the fortified headlands of Ros bhàn and Ceann leathan stand to either side of it.
36.known_for: the gulf's chief harbour and fish-market

37.history: Seann Toll, old hollow, is named for the sea-caves under its headland, where Seann-Dhaoine marks are said to be cut into the rock. The Ròdaich resettled it in the Holy Age and it has been a fishing port ever since. It keeps the ancestor rite and the northern herring fleet.

38.history: Cuan bheag of the north-west was built by Tuathaich fishing families in the first years after the Severance, on a shore the Ròdaich had never settled. It is a village of boats and drying racks. It sells its catch through Caol mhòr.
38.known_for: Tuathaich fishing boats and drying racks

39.founded_by: Ròdaich ferrymen; resettled by the Tuathaich
39.history: Àth gheal was a Ròdaich ford-and-harbour town of the long quiet centuries, walled in the Age of Strangers and resettled by the Tuathaich after the Severance. When the dubhan economy came it was among the northern towns that went on working the last coal seams. It was one of the holdouts broken in An Cogadh Fada, and its people still speak bitterly of that year.
39.known_for: a walled town of the coal-holdouts

40.founded_by: the garrison of the gulf mouth
40.history: Ros bhàn is a fortified headland at the mouth of the gulf, walled and given a citadel in the long quiet centuries to guard the harbours within. It is a city by rank, though most of its people are soldiers, customs clerks and their families. The white stone of its headland gives it its name.
40.known_for: fortified headland at the gulf mouth

41.history: Cnoc chaol, the narrow hill, is a small herding town of the north. It is not the southern Cnoc chaol that gave Tonn Mhòr its name. Its people keep Feallsanachd an Fhèidh and send their cheese and kids to the market at Baile gharbh.

42.history: Ceann bheag is a citadel harbour of the north-east, a Holy Age landing that grew with the coastal trade. Its citadel was raised in the Age of Strangers to guard the anchorage the human ships used. The villages of Ceann thais and Achadh fhiadhaich lie within its province and send their goods through its quays.

43.history: Ceann ghorm, the blue headland, is a river town on the Abhainn chaol in the east whose pilots have long guided boats up from Seann Mhorn on the coast to the landings of Seann Dunn and Ros fhionn. It was founded in the long quiet centuries and grew in the Age of Strangers. Its people follow Feallsanachd an Fhèidh.
43.known_for: river pilots of the Abhainn chaol

44.history: Baile thais stands where the Abhainn uaine reaches the gulf, and the river landing of Cidhe Beag lies just upstream. Boats have been launched here since the Holy Age to carry goods inland and ore down. It is a busy, unwalled town of boatmen and warehouses.
44.known_for: Cidhe Beag landing on the Abhainn uaine

45.history: Baile ghlas is a great harbour town on the capital shore and the seat of its province. Its rope-walks and sail-lofts have fitted ships for the capital since the Holy Age, and it claims, with no record to prove it, to have rigged the Sundering fleet. It has never been walled; the capital's walls stand close by.

46.history: Àth fhionn, the fair ford, is a large inland town at the crossing of the southern drove road. It has been a resting place for herds and drovers since the Holy Age. Its people keep the ancestor rite and hold the drove-road fair at the ford.
46.known_for: fording place of the southern drove road

47.history: Seann Bhral of the west coast is a Seann-Dhaoine site the Ròdaich resettled in the Holy Age. It grew into a large port on the western sea roads and took up the Yellow Scorpion faith, which is strong along this coast. Its harbour is unwalled, trusting to the citadel at Ros bheag to the north.
47.known_for: west-coast harbour of the Scorpion faith

48.history: Baile naomh, the holy town, grew around wells in the vein country that the Holy Age custodians held sacred. The hot springs of Muileann ruadh lie to the west and the silver workings of Muileann chiar to the north-west. It is a small town of shrines and lodging houses, keeping the ancestor rite.
48.known_for: holy wells of the vein country

49.history: Caol fhiadhaich is a harbour on a rough strait of the west coast, within the province of Inis thais. It was founded in the long quiet centuries by fishers who braved waters the older harbours avoided. Its people keep the Direwolf's faith.

50.history: Àth gharbh, the rough ford, is a walled town of the south-west, a short walk from Doire shean and its great roadside tavern, Am Buabhall Fortanach. That tavern fortified with the others of the old mining circuit before the war of the Severance. Since An Cogadh Fada, A' chiad chabhlach has been stationed here and carries the town's name.
50.known_for: the First Fleet's walled ford town

51.history: Cill àrsaidh of the north is an old cell of the ancestor rite, founded in the Holy Age and never much more than a village around its shrine. It lies inland of the Hawk bay and has kept to the older faith while its neighbours took up Mòd. The shrine keepers are hereditary.
51.known_for: ancient cell of the ancestor rite

52.history: Cnoc ìseal, the low hill, is a small town of the north-east given to flax and linen. It was founded in the long quiet centuries and has changed little since. It follows Feallsanachd an Fhèidh.

53.history: Cill àrsaidh of Cuan ghlas is an old cell that the teachers of Feallsanachd an Fhèidh took as a retreat early in the school's history. It became a large village of students and farmers. The school's dormant teachers kept it alive through the Age of Strangers, and it filled again at the revival.

54.founded_by: Ròdaich millers; resettled by the Tuathaich
54.history: Muileann àrsaidh, the ancient mill, is the seat of its province in the Tuathaich north-west, founded as a Ròdaich mill town in the Holy Age. It was walled in the Age of Strangers and resettled by the Tuathaich after the Severance. The mill still grinds for the surrounding villages.
54.known_for: the old mill of the north-west

55.history: Inis àrsaidh is an island town on the Abhainn naomh in the west, founded in the Holy Age; its ships put to sea from Ros àrsaidh at the river mouth. It was the nearest river port to the field of Àth leathan, and in An Cogadh Fada it supplied the state's forces for the first battle. Its fairground is one of the two grounds where the travelling circus, An Siorcas Siubhail Do-thuigsinn, pitches.
55.known_for: river port near the field of Àth leathan

56.history: Doire fhionn of Caol shean is an oak-grove village on the way to Allt an Àigh. Pilgrims to the stream have lodged in its houses since the Holy Age, and the Library at Muileann chaol stands on the road to the north. Its people follow Feallsanachd an Fhèidh.
56.known_for: oak grove on the pilgrims' way

57.history: Ros fhionn of Caol shean is a citadel town on the Abhainn chaol in the east, near the stream of Allt an Àigh. It is where most pilgrims to the stream come ashore from the river boats that bring them up from Seann Mhorn, and its citadel was raised in the Age of Sundering to guard them. It is not the Ros fhionn of the old bridge, which lies to the north.
57.known_for: river landing of the Allt an Àigh pilgrims

58.founded_by: a human milling concern with Ròdaich labour
58.history: Muileann uaine was built in the Age of Strangers as a crushing mill for ore from the interior workings. It is not the Muileann uaine of the Cnoc bheag country that the Green Death struck, though the two are often confused. It is a small town now and keeps the orthodox Obsidian Rite.
58.known_for: ore-crushing mill of the interior workings

59.history: Doire ghorm is a grove village of the south-east, founded by charcoal-burners in the long quiet centuries. Its charcoal once fed the smithies of the south coast. It keeps the orthodox Obsidian Rite, like its neighbours.

60.founded_by: Ròdaich fishers; resettled by the Tuathaich
60.history: Ros mhòr of the north-west is a harbour on a great headland, founded by Ròdaich fishers in the long quiet centuries. After the Severance it was resettled by the Tuathaich and grew with the northern trade. It lies between the harbours of Caol mhòr and Caol naomh.
60.known_for: big headland harbour of the Tuathaich

61.history: Cnoc fhionn, the fair hill, is a large town of orchards and farms in the north-east. It has been settled since the Holy Age and keeps the ancestor rite. Its apples and cider go down to the harbour at Seann Tarr.

62.history: Inis bheag is an island town on the Abhainn bheag in the north-east and the seat of its province. Its boatyards have built fishing craft for the coast since the Holy Age and send them down the river to the sea at Caol chrom. It follows Feallsanachd an Fhèidh and shares its river with Ros fhionn of the old bridge.

63.history: Ros bheag is the citadel harbour and provincial seat of the western coast, holding Dùn thais and Ros àrsaidh within its province. It was fortified in the Holy Age and has been the western sea's naval station through every age since. Its people keep the Yellow Scorpion faith.
63.known_for: citadel harbour of the western coast

64.history: Seann Warr is a Seann-Dhaoine harbour on the capital's western shore, resettled by the Ròdaich and walled in the Holy Age. Its citadel guards the western approaches to the capital. An còigeamh rèisimeid, raised in An Cogadh Fada, is stationed here and carries its name.

65.history: Cnoc àrsaidh of Dùn ìseal is a hill town crowned by old cairns, above Baile naomh. It has been a shepherding place since the Holy Age. Its people keep the ancestor rite and tend the cairns at the turning of the seasons.

66.history: Àth fhiadhaich of the south-west is a ford on the pilgrimage road from Caol leathan to the temple at Inis thais. It grew from a single house of the long quiet centuries into a small town that lives on the pilgrims. It keeps the Direwolf's faith.
66.known_for: ford on the Direwolf pilgrims' road

67.history: The southern Àth shean is the larger of the two, a great ford town near the south coast. It has been a market since the Holy Age and has never needed walls. Its harbour is the old site of Seann Chwen, a short way east.

68.history: Baile fhiadhaich of Cnoc gheal is a walled farm town of the north-east. It was founded in the long quiet centuries and walled in the Age of Strangers against raiders from the sea. It keeps the ancestor rite.
68.known_for: walled farm town of the north-east

69.founded_by: the garrison of the north-coast road
69.history: Cnoc uaine of Caol ìseal is a hill fort over the north-coast road, raised in the long quiet centuries and walled since. Its garrison watched the road through the Age of Strangers. It keeps the ancestor rite.
69.known_for: hill fort over the north-coast road

70.history: Cnoc gheal is a white hill with a small citadel, raised as a watchtower in the long quiet centuries to give warning of ships on the northern coast. Its fire could be seen from Cill leathan and Àth fhionn, and the three kept a common watch. It follows Feallsanachd an Fhèidh, and its garrison is now a handful of old soldiers and their families.
70.known_for: white-hill watchtower of the north coast

71.history: Baile Mòr dhìreach of Caol bheag is a walled town with a citadel, built by Holy Age custodians where the north-eastern road runs straight. It is small for a city, but it holds the road and the market between Inis mhòr and Baile gharbh. It follows Feallsanachd an Fhèidh.
71.known_for: walled town on the straight road

72.history: Achadh fhiadhaich is a village of the north-east, founded in the long quiet centuries on wild pasture that no earlier people had fenced. It breeds horses and grows hay for the coast, and the carters of Ceann bheag have bought its horses for generations. It follows Feallsanachd an Fhèidh.

73.founded_by: Ròdaich fishers; resettled by the Tuathaich
73.history: Cnoc bhàn of the north-west is a harbour facing the pirate waters. It was founded by Ròdaich fishers in the long quiet centuries and resettled by the Tuathaich after the Severance. Its boats avoid the waters where old sailors place the Sea-Watcher.

74.founded_by: millers of the northern mining road
74.history: Muileann fhada, the long mill, is a small walled town on the old mining road of the north. An Taigh-seinnse Reòta stands at its edge, one of the great taverns of the old circuit. Colbh Cnoc chiar stands to the west, and the town's people say the stone's two words are older than any mill.
74.known_for: An Taigh-seinnse Reòta on the mining road

75.history: Inis leathan is a village on a broad island off the north coast, founded in the long quiet centuries by ferrymen who ran boats to the mainland. In the Age of Strangers its ferry carried supplies to the tavern and mill at Muileann fhada. It still keeps the ferry, and little else.

76.history: Ros fhionn of Inis bheag is a walled city on a headland over the Abhainn bheag, founded in the Holy Age where the first bridges crossed the river. Drochaid Ros fhionn, the old crossing, is still standing but has seen little traffic since the local trade dried up. Its temple is a hall of Feallsanachd an Fhèidh.
76.known_for: Drochaid Ros fhionn, the old bridge

77.history: Dùn thais of the north-east is a great hill city with a citadel and a temple, the chief place of its province. It lies close to Leabharlann Muileann chaol, and many of the Library's clerks and copyists live in it. It follows Feallsanachd an Fhèidh.
77.known_for: great hill city near the Library

78.history: Muileann chiar of Achadh shean stands at the edge of Coille Naomh Muileann chiar, the forest marked sacred before any faith claimed it. Its people were party to the holy-wood dispute of the Holy Age and have kept the forest's edge since. Tiormachd Achadh shean, the Long Drought, struck it in the Age of Strangers. It is not the silver town of the same name.
78.known_for: keepers of the sacred forest's edge

79.history: Cnoc dhearg of Muileann naomh is a small town of the west, founded in the long quiet centuries on a hill of red clay. Its potteries supply jars and tiles to the western harbours, and the Age of Strangers brought it a brief trade in crucibles for the assayers. It keeps the Yellow Scorpion faith.

80.history: Ceann gheal is a harbour town north of the capital, founded in the long quiet centuries. The hollow called Toll-dubh lies in the hills behind it; it has never been mapped, and the town's people do not go near it. It keeps the capital's faith.
80.known_for: white headland and the Toll-dubh hollow

81.history: Doire dhearg began as a mining camp in the Age of Strangers, when the interior was first worked by the ton. Its red spoil-heaps are still visible above the village. Many of its people left when the workings moved on, and the village that remains keeps the ancestor rite.
81.known_for: red spoil-heaps of the camp years

82.history: Achadh fhada, the long field, is a village of barley farms in the capital's southern country. It was founded in the long quiet centuries and has changed little since. It keeps the Direwolf's faith, unlike most of its neighbours.

83.history: Cnoc ruadh of Cathair fhada is a hill town on the south road, founded in the long quiet centuries by herders who grazed the red hill. It grew as a stopping place between the southern ford towns and the capital. Its people keep the capital's faith and sell hides at the market of Àth shean.
83.known_for: red-hill pasture on the south road

84.history: Ceann thais is a harbour village of the north-east, best known for An Leòmhann Buidhe, one of the great taverns of the old mining circuit, which stands at its edge. It was founded in the long quiet centuries. It follows Feallsanachd an Fhèidh.
84.known_for: An Leòmhann Buidhe, the Yellow Lion

85.founded_by: Ròdaich ferrymen; resettled by the Tuathaich
85.history: Caol naomh, the holy strait, is a harbour of the north-west founded by Ròdaich ferrymen in the Holy Age, who held the crossing sacred and blessed each boat before it put out. It was resettled by the Tuathaich after the Severance, and the new ferrymen kept the blessing without the old words. It keeps the Yellow Scorpion faith.

86.history: Caol ìseal is a harbour town on a low strait of the north coast and the seat of its province. Its salt pans have supplied the northern fisheries since the Holy Age. It keeps the ancestor rite.
86.known_for: salt pans of the low strait

87.history: Ros dhìreach of Cnoc bheag is a walled fishing village on the north-central coast, founded in the long quiet centuries. A' Phlàigh Uaine, the Green Death, struck it in the Age of Strangers. It was walled after the Severance, when the Tuathaich coast became a frontier. It keeps the Hawk's rite.
87.known_for: walled fishing village of the Hawk coast

88.history: Ceann àrsaidh is a walled river city on an ancient headland over the Abhainn fhionn, east of the capital. It has been a river port since the Holy Age, and its barges run down to Cathair dhomhain at the river mouth, the gateway to the eastern sea road. An Taigh-seinnse Mòr stands on the road to the west.
88.known_for: ancient headland on the river road to the eastern sea

89.history: Cnoc ìseal of Doire mhin is a small town of hill farms east of the capital, founded in the long quiet centuries. The field of Muileann ghlas, where An Cogadh Fada ended, lies just to the west, and the town's barns sheltered the wounded after the battle. It keeps the capital's faith.
89.known_for: hill farms by Muileann ghlas field

90.history: Ros gharbh is a harbour town on a rough headland of the gulf and the seat of its province. It was founded in the long quiet centuries and grew with the gulf's fishing fleet. It keeps the capital's faith.

91.founded_by: the garrison of the capital's south road
91.history: Cnoc ìseal of Baile chiar is a walled hill on the capital's south road, founded in the long quiet centuries as a watch-post over the southern farms. Its walls were strengthened in the war of the Severance. It is a small town now, keeping the capital's faith and a toll it no longer collects.
91.known_for: walled hill on the capital's south road

92.history: Inis chrom is a large walled harbour on a bent island of the south-west. It has been a port since the Holy Age and its sailors keep the Direwolf's faith. It lies close to Am Buabhall Fortanach and Àth gharbh.
92.known_for: bent isle harbour and Direwolf sailors

93.history: Àth fhionn of Seann Skell is a ford town of the south-east. It was founded in the long quiet centuries. Since An Cogadh Fada it has billeted soldiers of the regiments stationed at Seann Skell nearby. It keeps the orthodox Obsidian Rite.
93.known_for: ford town beside the Seann Skell garrisons

94.history: Seann Vell of the south-east is a citadel harbour on a Seann-Dhaoine site, resettled by the Ròdaich in the Holy Age. Its citadel guards the south-eastern coast and the approach to Seann Bhral, its larger neighbour and old rival. It keeps the ancestor rite.

95.founded_by: Ròdaich harbour-folk; resettled by the Tuathaich
95.history: Caol mhòr, the great strait, was a Ròdaich harbour of the Holy Age. After the Severance it became the chief port of the Tuathaich, and it is now their largest town. Its yards take timber from Doire mhin, and its people keep the Yellow Scorpion faith.

96.history: Doire ruadh is a village of red oaks inland of the Hawk bay, founded in the long quiet centuries by families who kept hawks for the rite of Mòd. Its birds are still flown at the rite's gatherings in Cnoc bheag. Since the Severance it has lain close to the Tuathaich border and has seen more soldiers than it wishes.

97.history: Seann Vell of Baile mhin is a small river landing on a Seann-Dhaoine site on the Abhainn bheag in the north-east, a short way above the river mouth at Caol chrom, resettled by the Ròdaich in the Holy Age. It lives on the seal-hunt at the river mouth and the fishing. It follows Feallsanachd an Fhèidh.

98.history: Muileann leathan of the north-west was built by Tuathaich settlers soon after the Severance to grind grain for the northern villages, which had lost the Ròdaich mills to the south. It is a small town, and its mill-race was dug by hand by the first households. It keeps the Yellow Scorpion faith.

99.history: Cnoc ruadh of Achadh chaol is a hill town of the eastern uplands, a sheep town since the Holy Age. Its wool goes down to Cuan ruadh for shipping. It keeps the ancestor rite.
99.known_for: red-hill sheepwalks and Cuan ruadh wool

100.history: Àth chrom, the bent ford, is a river town at a bend of the Abhainn naomh in the west, below Seann Skell, whose boats go down to the sea at Ros àrsaidh. It was founded in the long quiet centuries. Since An Cogadh Fada, troops of the regiment named for Seann Skell have been quartered close by.
100.known_for: bent ford on the lower Abhainn naomh

101.history: Doire mhòr was cut out of a great oak wood in the Age of Strangers, when the workings east of the capital needed pit-props faster than any Holy Age forester would have felled them. The wood is gone and the village farms the clearing.
101.known_for: pit-props from a vanished oak wood

102.history: Doire fhiadhaich of Cnoc dhubh is a village only by the old rank; it is large, and it has a citadel raised by the Holy Age custodians who held these hills. Làrach an Teampaill lies in the hills to its east. Its people keep the ancestor rite and will not cut the oaks nearest the ruin.

103.history: Inis uaine is a river town on a green island in the Abhainn chaol in the east, founded in the long quiet centuries; its boats go down to the sea at Seann Mhorn. After An Cogadh Fada, An t-ochdamh rèisimeid was stationed here and took the town's name, and the barracks have changed the town's trade from fish to soldiers' wants. It keeps the ancestor rite.

104.founded_by: Ròdaich custodians of the capital's east
104.history: Cuan uaine, whose name means the green harbour, is a walled temple city on the Abhainn fhionn east of the capital, fortified in the Holy Age to guard the river road to the eastern shore. Its temple of the Dark Unicorn is much visited by those who cannot reach the capital's. The barracks town of Inis mhòr lies just upriver to the north.
104.known_for: the temple of Uallach on the Abhainn fhionn

105.history: Baile dhìreach, the straight town, is a harbour on the west coast built around one long street to the quay. It was founded in the long quiet centuries by traders of the Yellow Scorpion faith, among Direwolf neighbours. The two faiths have shared its market without any trouble the rolls think worth noting.
105.known_for: straight-street harbour of the Scorpion faith

106.founded_by: farmers of the capital's southern country
106.history: Baile chiar, the dusky town, is the market and provincial seat of the capital's southern country. It has been a farm market since the Holy Age and has never been walled; the citadel at Baile àrsaidh stands close by. Grain from Achadh fhada and the southern farms comes to its market.
106.known_for: market of the capital's southern country

107.history: Cnoc chrom was built in the Age of Strangers as a depot on the ore road from the interior to the gulf. It was walled in the years before the war of the Severance, when the mining roads began to arm themselves. It is a small town now and keeps the capital's faith.
107.known_for: walled depot of the ore road

108.history: Àth dhearg of Cnoc shean began as a mining camp at a ford in the Age of Strangers, and its red water is said to come from the spoil. It is neither the Àth dhearg whose name the northern lighthouse bears nor the western ford that the Great Hunger struck.
108.known_for: red ford of the mining camps

109.history: Cill thais, the damp cell, is a large village and the seat of its province, founded in the Holy Age beside Coille Naomh Cnoc bheag. The forest is sacred to the Dark Unicorn and has never been settled, logged or fully mapped, and the village's wardens keep others out of it under the division of custody that settled the holy-wood dispute. In the Age of Strangers the wardens refused the timber contracts, and the record does not say how they were allowed to.
109.known_for: wardens of Coille Naomh Cnoc bheag

110.history: Seann Bhral of the south-east is a Seann-Dhaoine site that the Ròdaich resettled in the Holy Age, and it has grown into the greatest harbour of that coast and the seat of its province. It was walled in the Age of Strangers, when its quays shipped ore from the interior. It keeps the ancestor rite.

111.founded_by: the watch of the deep strait
111.history: Caol dhomhain is a harbour village on a deep strait of the south-east, with a citadel raised in the long quiet centuries to watch it. The village is small and the citadel is its reason. It keeps the ancestor rite.

112.founded_by: human settlers from an Tìr Thall
112.history: Baile leathan was built by human settlers in the Age of Strangers on the northern coast, one of the few places the strangers founded rather than took. After the Severance it became a Tuathaich town. It keeps the Tuathaich folk tradition and its oldest families still count their descent from the Crossing.
112.known_for: an old strangers' settlement of the north

113.history: Àth fhionn of Muileann shean is a ford town of the north coast, founded in the long quiet centuries where the coast road crosses a clear river. It shares the watch-fire of Cnoc gheal and trades with the harbour of Cill leathan. It follows Feallsanachd an Fhèidh.
113.known_for: fair ford of the north coast

114.founded_by: Ròdaich weavers; resettled by the Tuathaich
114.history: Àth uaine of Cnoc ghorm is a green ford of the north-west, founded by Ròdaich flax-weavers in the Holy Age. It was resettled by the Tuathaich after the Severance and still weaves. It keeps the Yellow Scorpion faith.

115.history: Muileann ruadh of Doire fhionn is a mill town of the north-central country, founded in the Holy Age. Its citadel was raised after the Severance to watch the Tuathaich border. It keeps the Hawk's rite.

116.founded_by: Ròdaich herders; resettled by the Tuathaich
116.history: Cnoc uaine of Muileann àrsaidh is a green hill of the north-west, founded by Ròdaich herders in the long quiet centuries. It was resettled by the Tuathaich after the Severance. It is a grazing town and keeps the Yellow Scorpion faith.

117.history: Doire fhionn of the east is the seat of its province, a great village of the Holy Age in an oak grove, which has never been raised to the rank of town despite its size. Its oaks are managed under rules older than the kingdom. It keeps the ancestor rite, and the old field-village of Achadh àrsaidh lies to its north.
117.known_for: great oak grove of the east

118.history: Baile Mòr uaine is a walled city with a citadel in the north-eastern hills, founded in the Holy Age. It follows Feallsanachd an Fhèidh and is among its strongholds. Its walls were repaired in the Age of Strangers.

119.history: Cuan ruadh is the easternmost harbour of the island and the seat of its province, a port since the Holy Age. Its boats go out further than any on the coast, and it has lost more to pirates than any other eastern town. It keeps the ancestor rite.

120.history: Muileann mhin of Baile fhiadhaich is a mill town of the west, founded in the long quiet centuries on a stream that turns smooth stones. It grinds for the harbour at Baile fhiadhaich. It keeps the Yellow Scorpion faith, and its millers are known for honest measures.

121.history: Muileann gharbh, the rough mill, was built in the Age of Strangers to crush ore on the road down to the eastern harbours. When the mountain was worked day and night the mill never stopped, and the town grew no larger than the mill needed. It follows Feallsanachd an Fhèidh, which found many hearers among the mill hands.
121.known_for: rough mill of the ore road

122.history: Ros àrsaidh is a small walled harbour on an ancient headland of the west, fortified by the Holy Age custodians. It lies within the province of Ros bheag and has always stood in the shadow of that citadel. It keeps the Yellow Scorpion faith.
122.known_for: walled harbour on the ancient headland

123.history: Cill ghlas, the grey cell, was a quiet village of Feallsanachd an Fhèidh in the hills east of the capital until the Age of Strangers pushed the workings under it. Late in that age a routine excavation tore open a fault around it, killing dozens and closing the working; the Rending gave the island the word 'scàinte'. The village was rebuilt on the far side of the crack, and its people still mark the day of the dead.

124.history: Àth uaine of Cnoc dhubh began as a mining camp at a ford in the Age of Strangers. Its camp graves lie in the field by the ford, tended by the ancestor rite's keepers. The camp outlived its working and became a small farm town.
124.known_for: camp graves by the green ford

125.history: Baile ruadh is a farm town near the eastern coast, founded in the long quiet centuries. Since the lighthouses were built its people have supplied the keepers of Taigh-solais Baile ìseal on the coast beyond. It keeps the ancestor rite.

126.history: Ceann leathan of the east is a harbour town and the seat of its province, founded in the Holy Age on a broad headland facing the open sea. It is not the gulf city of the melee, and its people resent the confusion. It keeps the ancestor rite and a fishing fleet that works as far south as the waters off Seann Bhral.
126.known_for: broad headland harbour of the east

127.history: Seann Vell of the west coast is a small harbour on a Seann-Dhaoine site, the seat of its province. It was resettled by the Ròdaich in the Holy Age and took up the Yellow Scorpion faith with the rest of the coast. An ceathramh cabhlach is stationed at Cuan shean, a short way up the coast.
127.known_for: old harbour of the west coast

128.history: Seann Warr of Àth chiar is a small harbour on a Seann-Dhaoine landing on the south shore of the gulf. The Ròdaich resettled it in the Holy Age. It keeps the ancestor rite and a few boats, and pays its dues to the larger harbours across the water.
128.known_for: old landing on the gulf's south shore

129.history: Cnoc shean, the old hill, is a small town of the south, settled since the Holy Age. Its common holds the market of the farms around it. It keeps the capital's faith.
129.known_for: market common on the old hill

130.history: Dùn thais of the north is the northernmost Ròdaich citadel, raised by the Holy Age custodians on the northern coast. Since the Severance it has watched the Tuathaich country. It keeps the ancestor rite.

131.history: Baile gharbh is a large market town of the north-east and the seat of its province. It has been a wool market since the Holy Age, and the hill towns of Cnoc chaol and Àth fhada bring their flocks and cheese to it. It follows Feallsanachd an Fhèidh and has no walls, trusting to Baile Mòr dhìreach close by.

132.history: Seann Skell of the Hawk bay is a walled harbour city on a Seann-Dhaoine site, sharing its bay with Ros gheal and Ros leathan. It was resettled by the Ròdaich in the Holy Age and walled in the Age of Sundering. It keeps the Hawk's rite.
132.known_for: walled old harbour of the Hawk bay

133.founded_by: the garrison of the bent strait
133.history: Caol chrom is a fortified harbour on a bent strait of the north-east, walled and given a citadel in the long quiet centuries. It is a city by rank but small in people, and its garrison has always outnumbered its fishermen. It follows Feallsanachd an Fhèidh.

134.history: Baile fhiadhaich of the west is a large harbour town and the seat of its province, founded in the Holy Age. It lies near the field of Àth leathan, and its people remember the first battle of An Cogadh Fada. It keeps the Yellow Scorpion faith.

135.history: Achadh dhomhain of Muileann chrom is a large farming village in deep fields, founded in the Holy Age. Its granaries fed the mining camps in the Age of Strangers and were requisitioned in the war of the Severance. It keeps the capital's faith.

136.history: Baile Mòr dhìreach of Baile chaol is a citadel city on the eastern straight road, founded in the Holy Age to hold the road between the vein country and the coast. It was a tithe station in the Age of Strangers, and the ledgers kept there were among those burned in the raids before the Severance. It keeps the ancestor rite.
136.known_for: citadel city of the eastern road

137.history: Muileann mhin is a large river town on the Abhainn fhionn east of the capital and the seat of its province. Its flour mills have fed the capital since the Holy Age. It keeps the capital's faith and ships its flour down the river to Cathair dhomhain and along the shore to Cathair dhearg and Ros dhomhain.

138.history: Cill bhàn, the white cell, is a village of the ancestor rite in the east, founded in the Holy Age. It lies near the hot springs and the silver workings of the vein country. It has kept its shrine through every age and every change of master.
138.known_for: white cell of the ancestor rite

139.history: Seann Chwen of Àth shean is a harbour on the south coast, on a Seann-Dhaoine site. It was resettled by the Ròdaich in the Holy Age and is the port for the southern Àth shean. It keeps the capital's faith.

140.founded_by: Ròdaich herders; resettled by the Tuathaich
140.history: Cnoc mhòr of Doire ghlas is a Tuathaich town of the north coast, founded by Ròdaich herders in the long quiet centuries and resettled after the Severance. Its people supply the keepers of Taigh-solais Muileann bheag. It keeps the Tuathaich folk tradition.
140.known_for: keepers of the Muileann bheag light

141.history: Cill leathan is a large harbour village of the north coast, founded as a cell in the Holy Age. A citadel was raised over its harbour in the Age of Strangers to guard the human ships that used it. It follows Feallsanachd an Fhèidh.
141.known_for: broad cell and its sea citadel

142.founded_by: Ròdaich farmers; resettled by the Tuathaich
142.history: Cnoc ghorm of the north-west is the inland seat of its province and one of the largest Tuathaich towns. It was a Ròdaich farm town of the Holy Age, resettled after the Severance. It is not the place of the stone Calbh Cnoc ghorm, which lies far to the south-east.

143.founded_by: Ròdaich fishers; resettled by the Tuathaich
143.history: Ceann mhòr is a great harbour on a headland of the north-west, under the beacon of Taigh-solais Baile chrom. It was a Ròdaich port of the Holy Age, struck by Gorta Baile chrom in the Age of Strangers and resettled by the Tuathaich after the Severance. It keeps the Yellow Scorpion faith.
143.known_for: great headland harbour under the Baile chrom light

144.history: Baile mhin is a river town on the Abhainn bheag in the north-east and the seat of its province, founded in the Holy Age. Its quays are sheltered and its trade steady, and its barges go down to Caol chrom at the river mouth. It follows Feallsanachd an Fhèidh, and the old landing of Seann Vell lies within its province.
144.known_for: sheltered river quays of the north-east

145.history: Achadh naomh is a large village and the seat of its province in the north-central country, founded in the Holy Age on a field held sacred. Colbh Cnoc chiar stands to its east, carved 'remember the fire'. It keeps the ancestor rite.
145.known_for: holy field by Colbh Cnoc chiar

146.founded_by: hosts of the Allt an Àigh pilgrims
146.history: Achadh dhomhain of Caol shean is a large village beside Allt an Àigh, the stream of fortune. Pilgrims have come to drink from it since the Holy Age, and the village lives on them. It follows Feallsanachd an Fhèidh.
146.known_for: hosts to Allt an Àigh pilgrims

147.history: Doire ghlas of Cnoc dhubh is a village of grey oaks near Làrach an Teampaill. It was founded in the Holy Age, and its people have guided visitors to the ruin ever since. It keeps the ancestor rite.
147.known_for: grey oaks by Làrach an Teampaill

148.founded_by: herders of the Doire uaine hills
148.history: Doire uaine is a small village in the hills where inscriptions describe the Hollow Man, something that walked without breathing and attacked anyone who lit a fire in its sight. The village was founded in the Holy Age. It follows Feallsanachd an Fhèidh.
148.known_for: the Hollow Man of the hills

149.history: Doire fhada, the long grove, is a walled village of the capital shore, founded in the long quiet centuries. It was walled in the Age of Strangers to protect its grain stores. It keeps the capital's faith.

150.history: Achadh mhin is a farming village of the south, founded in the Holy Age. Tonn Mhòr struck it in the first years of the restored kingdom and destroyed it in a single night. It was rebuilt and keeps the capital's faith.

151.history: Muileann òg, the young mill, was built in the first years of the restored kingdom. Its annual fair, Fèill Muileann òg, became the island's largest gathering. The field of Muileann ghlas, where An Cogadh Fada ended, lies close by.
151.known_for: Fèill Muileann òg, the great fair

152.history: Ros dhìreach of Cnoc mhòr is a harbour on a straight headland of the gulf, founded in the long quiet centuries. It is a city by rank and the harbour of Cnoc mhòr's cattle trade. It keeps the capital's faith.

153.history: Cnoc bheag of Muileann shean is a small town of hill farms on the north coast, founded in the long quiet centuries. It follows Feallsanachd an Fhèidh. Its people send their sons to the Feallsanachd teachers at Cill àrsaidh.

154.founded_by: human settlers from an Tìr Thall
154.history: Cnoc ghlas of Àth àrsaidh was settled by humans in the Age of Strangers and became a Tuathaich town after the Severance. It keeps the Tuathaich folk tradition, and its singers are among the keepers of the First Canoe fragment.
154.known_for: strangers' settlement on the grey hill

155.history: Cnoc ghorm of Doire fhionn is a town of the north-central country, founded in the Holy Age. It keeps the ancestor rite and its bees, whose wax lit the shrines at Cill àrsaidh before dubhan lamps came.

156.history: Àth uaine of Seann Skell is a ford town inland of the Hawk bay, founded in the Holy Age. It keeps the ancestor rite. It is the market for the three quarrelling harbours of the bay.
156.known_for: green ford inland of Seann Skell

157.history: Àth fhada, the long ford, is a town on the north-east road, founded in the Holy Age. It follows Feallsanachd an Fhèidh. Its ford is long and shallow, and carts cross it only at low water.
157.known_for: long ford of the north-east road

158.history: Inis naomh is a walled harbour on a holy isle of the north coast, founded in the Holy Age. It follows Feallsanachd an Fhèidh. Its walls were built to keep the isle's shrine safe from raiders.
158.known_for: holy isle and its walled landing

159.history: Àth gheal of Muileann bheag is a ford town near Seann Tarr, founded in the long quiet centuries. It keeps the ancestor rite. At the great feasts it lodges the pilgrims bound for the shrine at Seann Tarr.

160.founded_by: human administrators of the northern landing
160.history: Muileann fhionn was built as a fort and mill by human administrators in the Age of Strangers, to guard the northern landing. After the Severance it became a Tuathaich town. It keeps the Yellow Scorpion faith.

161.founded_by: Ròdaich fishers of the Hawk bay
161.history: Ros leathan is a harbour town on the Hawk bay, sharing it with Ros gheal and Seann Skell. It was founded in the long quiet centuries by fishers who would not pay Ros gheal's mooring dues. It keeps the Hawk's rite.
161.known_for: rival wharves of the Hawk bay

162.history: Seann Vell of the capital's east is a walled river town on a Seann-Dhaoine site on the Abhainn fhionn and the seat of its province. It was resettled by the Ròdaich in the Holy Age. An Taigh-seinnse Mòr stands just east of it, at the river quay of Cuan chrom.
162.known_for: walled river town on the Cuan chrom road

163.history: Àth chiar is a ford town east of the capital, founded in the long quiet centuries. The field of Muileann ghlas lies to its south-west, and the town was a supply post in the last battle of An Cogadh Fada. It keeps the capital's faith.
163.known_for: dusky ford near Muileann ghlas field

164.history: Doire chaol was laid out after the Severance on a narrow oak strip south of the capital, to house the families of the royal household. It grew into a large village and the seat of its province. It keeps the capital's faith.

165.history: Cnoc dhubh of Achadh àrsaidh is a black hill with a citadel, south-east of the capital, founded in the Holy Age. Coille Naomh Cnoc bheag lies to its west and the field of Muileann ghlas to its east. It keeps the capital's faith.
165.known_for: black-hill citadel south of the capital

166.history: Inis thais is a walled temple city of the south-west and the seat of its province. Its temple of Clach, the Resplendent Direwolf, is the chief shrine of that faith, and pilgrims come to it from Caol leathan and the whole western coast. It has been a holy city since the Holy Age.

167.history: Cnoc leathan is a large town and the seat of its province, on the south road of the east. An Taigh-òsta Grianach, one of the great inns of the old circuit, stands to its south. It keeps the ancestor rite.
167.known_for: An Taigh-òsta Grianach on the south road

168.history: Baile àrsaidh, the ancient town, is a citadel town of the capital's southern country, founded in the Holy Age. Its citadel guards the market at Baile chiar. It keeps the capital's faith.
168.known_for: old citadel of the southern country

169.history: Achadh fhionn is a village of the south-east, founded in the Holy Age in a fair field under Làrach an Dùin. It keeps the ancestor rite and leaves the ruin alone. Its people say the ruin was old when the first Ròdaich came.
169.known_for: fair field under Làrach an Dùin
